title: Nakhon Nayok With Kids: 2-Day Family Plan, Thailand | ThailandAddict
metaDesc: A family itinerary for Nakhon Nayok, Thailand with kids: shallow-pool swims at Nang Rong Waterfall, picnics at Wang Takrai Park, and the giant Ganesha shrine. Day-by-day timing, entry fees, and honest tips for traveling with children.

h1:
Nakhon Nayok With Kids
Waterfalls, Wang Takrai & the Ganesha Shrine in 2 Days, 1 Night
intro: Nakhon Nayok is one of the easiest provinces to take kids to if you're coming from Bangkok — it's an hour and a half by car. There are shallow waterfalls kids can wade into, shady parks for spreading out a picnic mat, and a giant Ganesha shrine where parents can stop to make a wish. We've built this as a 2-day, 1-night plan where everything sits close together, with no rushing, so there's room for naps and plenty of time in the water.

blocks.html: Traveling with kids isn't like a trip with friends — you have to leave room for bathroom stops and naps, and pick places where children can actually get in the water safely. Nakhon Nayok handles all of that well: the distances between stops are short, several waterfalls are shallow pools, and the riverside resorts aren't expensive. This plan keeps day one focused on water and nature, and day two on the shrine plus picking up snacks to take home before you head back.

blocks.text: Before you set off — what to pack when you have kids

items: A change of clothes + non-slip water shoes — the rocks at the falls get very slippery, and strapped water shoes help far more than flip-flops.
A mat + towels — some spots rent mats for around 30 THB, but bringing your own is more reassuring.
Snacks + drinking water — kids can get hungry on the road at any moment; having some in the car cuts down on the fussing.
Mosquito repellent + sunscreen — the area around the falls is shady, but the mosquitoes come out in force in the evening.
A waterproof phone pouch — handy for photos while everyone's in the water.

blocks.title: Pick the right season
blocks.html: Late rainy season into early winter (July–January) is when the waterfalls have the most water and run clearest. In the dry months (March–April) the flow can drop so low it's no fun. If you're coming specifically to swim with the kids, skipping the low-water stretch is worth it.

blocks.title: Book the activities in your Nakhon Nayok trip ahead
blocks.text: Booking online ahead on Klook or GetYourGuide is usually cheaper than the gate and skips the queue. Pick only the experiences you actually want — prices and availability are shown live on each site.

blocks.text: Day 1 — waterfall swim + Wang Takrai Park

blocks.label: Day 1
blocks.title: Swim at the falls, spread the mat, stay by the stream

items.activity: Leave Bangkok heading for Nakhon Nayok
items.note: It's about 130 km, an easy hour and a half. Setting off early makes it easier to find parking at the falls, and the kids are still fresh.

items.activity: Arrive at Nang Rong Waterfall, swim in the shallow pools
items.note: Nang Rong Waterfall sits within Khao Yai National Park, in Hin Tang sub-district, open 6:00 AM–6:00 PM. It has tiered shallow pools that are good for kids to wade into, plus shower rooms and toilets. Entry is around 50 THB per car, with an extra 10 THB per person.

items.activity: Take a break, change clothes, find lunch
items.note: There are restaurants and shops near the entrance. Order som tam and grilled chicken, or noodles, for an easy meal for the kids before moving on.

items.activity: Enter Wang Takrai Park, lay the mat under the trees
items.note: Wang Takrai is a forest park of over 1,500 rai where two streams meet — very shady. It's open 8:00 AM–6:00 PM, with entry at 150 THB per car (up to 8 passengers; an extra 10 THB per person beyond that). Mats rent for around 30 THB, and kids can soak comfortably along the stream.

items.activity: Stroll among the trees and flowers + let the kids run around
items.note: The grounds are wide and car-free — a good place to let kids run off some energy before evening.

items.activity: Check in at a riverside place to stay
items.note: Around the Sarika–Khun Dan Dam area there are plenty of riverside resorts. Many have stand-alone cabins where you can grill your own mu krata / barbecue. Prices start in the low thousands and suit families.

items.activity: Mu krata / grilled dinner by the water
items.note: Many resorts offer mu krata sets to order. The streamside setting is cool and pleasant, and once the kids have eaten they tend to fall asleep early.

blocks.title: Waterfalls with small children
blocks.html: Always check the water level before letting kids in. In the rainy season the water can rise fast and the rocks are slippery, so hold your child's hand the whole time and pick a shallow pool with a gentle current. Don't let them climb the high boulders.

blocks.text: Day 2 — the Ganesha shrine + snacks for the road home

blocks.label: Day 2
blocks.title: Make a wish at the shrine, visit a farm, buy snacks to take home

items.activity: Breakfast at the resort, pack up
items.note: No need to rush — let the kids eat their fill and take a short walk by the water before you go.

items.activity: Pay respects to Ganesha at Ganesha Park
items.note: Open 8:00 AM–6:00 PM. There are two giant stucco Ganesha statues (a seated, blessing-giving pose and a reclining pose), 9 meters across the lap and 15 meters tall, plus a museum of 108 poses to walk through. Kids get a thrill out of the giant statues while the grown-ups make their wishes.

items.activity: Stop at Eden Farm for some nature time
items.note: A farm out in the fields where you can take in rice-paddy views, snap photos, and kayak around the property. The kids get to see animals and nature up close.
Nakhon Nayok has plenty of streamside spots. Order grilled fish, tom yum, and som tam, and let the kids settle in to the sound of the water.

items.activity: Buy snacks to take home — madan, banana chips
items.note: Nakhon Nayok is known for sweet-pickled madan and processed namwa bananas. Stop at a snack shop around town before getting on the road back.
Leaving in the late afternoon helps you dodge the evening traffic on the way home, and the kids usually sleep most of the drive.

blocks.text: If your kids are older and want more of a thrill

blocks.html: Families with kids around 8 and up who can swim can add white-water rafting. Nakhon Nayok has rafting runs whose water level is regulated by the Khun Dan Prakan Chon Dam, so they run almost year-round and come in a range of difficulty levels, including easy ones for beginners. Ask about the minimum age and make sure every child wears a life jacket.

items.name: White-water rafting
items.blurb: Runs fed by the Khun Dan Dam, with easy levels for beginners. Older kids who can swim and wear a life jacket can join in.

items.name: ATV rides at the resort
items.blurb: Many resorts have an ATV track. Adults can take younger kids along as passengers at a slow speed.

items.name: Activity farms
items.blurb: Some parks and resorts offer kayaking, fishing, and cycling for kids to enjoy in a safe, enclosed area.

blocks.text: Rough budget per family (two parents + two kids)

items: Waterfall / park entry — Nang Rong is 50 THB per car plus per person; Wang Takrai is 150 THB per car. Around 250–300 THB total.
One night's stay — a riverside family cabin starts at around 1,200–2,500 THB depending on the season.
Food for two days — roughly 300–600 THB per meal, around 1,500–2,500 THB for the whole trip.
Whole trip — roughly 4,000–6,500 THB per family, up or down depending on where you stay and any add-on activities.

blocks.title: How to save a little more
blocks.html: If you book a place where you can grill your own, buying the mu krata ingredients and cooking them yourself is cheaper than ordering a ready-made set — and it's more of a family moment too.

faq.q: Is Nakhon Nayok doable with young kids?
faq.a: Easily. It's only about 130 km from Bangkok — an hour and a half by car — and the sights sit close together. Several waterfalls are shallow pools, and there are plenty of riverside family resorts to choose from. A 2-day, 1-night plan is just right and doesn't rush the kids.

faq.q: Which waterfall is best for kids to swim in?
faq.a: Nang Rong Waterfall has tiered shallow pools and full facilities, which makes it good for kids to get in. Wang Takrai is a shady forest park with a shallow stream to soak in and easy spots to spread a picnic mat. Both suit families, but always check the water level before getting in.

faq.q: How much is entry to Wang Takrai and Nang Rong Waterfall?
faq.a: Wang Takrai Park charges 150 THB per car (up to 8 passengers; an extra 10 THB per person beyond that). Nang Rong Waterfall is around 50 THB per car plus 10 THB per person. Prices can change, so it's worth confirming on site.

faq.q: What are the opening hours for the Ganesha shrine in Nakhon Nayok?
faq.a: Ganesha Park is open daily 8:00 AM–6:00 PM. It has two giant stucco Ganesha statues, 9 meters across the lap and 15 meters tall, plus a museum of 108 poses. Kids usually get a thrill out of the giant statues while the grown-ups make their wishes.

faq.q: What time of year is best to bring kids to swim at Nakhon Nayok's waterfalls?
faq.a: Late rainy season into early winter, roughly July through January, is when the water is highest and clearest, and the swimming is best. In the dry months of March–April the flow is usually low, so if you're set on swimming with the kids, it's best to avoid the low-water period.
